questions.q: Name the four primary supporting characters in "The Enemy" and state each one's relationship to Dr. Sadao.
questions.a: The four primary supporting characters are: (1) Hana — Sadao's wife, (2) Yumi — the nanny/servant, (3) The General — Sadao's patient and military superior, (4) Tom — the escaped American POW. A wrong answer (e.g., listing the professor or landlady as primary) reveals the student cannot distinguish between characters who appear in the present narrative versus those only in flashbacks/memories.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how Hana's attitude toward the wounded American changes from the moment they find him to the night he leaves.
questions.a: Initially Hana agrees with Sadao that putting him back in the sea is "the kindest thing," but she cannot move to do it. She then insists they carry him inside, washes him herself when Yumi refuses, assists with anesthesia during surgery, feeds him, and finally helps Sadao plan his escape. A wrong answer that says "she always wanted to help him" misses her initial repulsion and the crucial moment she overcomes it — showing the student hasn't traced her moral evolution.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "foil" to the old gardener: identify two specific statements he makes that directly contrast with Dr. Sadao's medical ethic, and explain the effect of this contrast.
questions.a: The gardener says: (1) "The white man ought to die. First he was shot. Then the sea caught him... If the master heals what the gun did and what the sea did they will take revenge on us." (2) "When the man was so near death why did he not let him bleed?" These contrast with Sadao's Hippocratic impulse to save life regardless of nationality. The effect: the gardener voices the nationalist/superstitious perspective that makes Sadao's choice isolation — the student who cannot quote these exact lines is relying on vague impression, not textual evidence.

questions.q: Analyze the General's character: is he a villain, a patriot, or a pragmatist? Support your judgment with three pieces of evidence from his dialogue and actions.
questions.a: The General is a self-absorbed pragmatist, not a villain or patriot. Evidence: (1) He admits "I thought of nothing but myself. In short, I forgot my promise to you" — confessing dereliction of duty. (2) He values Sadao's skill for his own survival: "N/A I trust... I do not care for their point of view." (3) He proposes assassination as a convenient solution: "It would be best if he could be quietly killed... by someone who does not know him." A student calling him "patriotic" ignores his explicit self-interest; calling him "villainous" misses his dark humor and human frailty.

questions.q: Evaluate Tom's role: does he exist only as a plot device to test Sadao, or does he have independent characterization? Defend your position with two textual details.
questions.a: Tom has independent characterization beyond being a test. Details: (1) He reveals scars on his neck from torture ("Those scars! What were they?"), giving him a backstory of suffering. (2) He expresses genuine gratitude and moral insight: "If all the Japs were like you there wouldn't have been a war" — showing he distinguishes individuals from stereotypes. A student who says "he's just a plot device" reduces a humanized enemy to a symbol, missing Buck's anti-war humanism.

questions.q: Create a 50-word diary entry from Yumi's perspective on the night the servants leave, capturing her conflict between loyalty to the children and patriotic conviction.
questions.a: "February 28. My heart breaks leaving Baby and Mistress. But I cannot stay where a white enemy is sheltered. The master heals the very people bombing our sons. The old gardener is right — the sea and gun tried to kill him; we defy the gods by saving him. I go home to pray for my country." A poor entry would focus only on the baby or only on patriotism, missing the *conflict* that defines her character.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of supporting characters examines how secondary figures — through their actions, dialogue, ______, and conflicts — reveal the protagonist's traits, advance the plot, and embody the story's themes.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a juror watching a trial: the ______ is the defendant, but the witnesses — Hana, the servants, the General, Tom — each give testimony that shapes the verdict.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can write a structured 150-word answer analyzing any supporting character using the PEEL method (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link), showing how that character's specific choices illuminate Dr.
